article.title: EUROPEAN TRANSPORT SYSTEMS 1990-2010

items.sentence_raw: It is difficult to conceive of vigorous economic growth without an efficient transport system.
Although modern information technologies can reduce the demand for physical transport by facilitating teleworking and teleservices, the requirement for transport continues to increase.
items.explain: Q22: The passage says *'Although modern information technologies can reduce the demand for physical transport... the requirement for transport continues to increase'*. This directly confirms that **the need for transport is growing, despite technological developments**. So the answer is **TRUE**.

items.sentence_raw: There are two key factors behind this trend.
For passenger transport, the determining factor is the spectacular growth in car use.
items.explain: Q14: Paragraph A talks about passenger transport and says *'the determining factor is the spectacular growth in car use'*. **'Spectacular growth'** means a very fast increase, which matches the heading **'the rapid growth of private transport'**. So the answer is **viii**.

items.sentence_raw: The number of cars on European Union
[EU] roads saw an increase of three million cars each year from 1990 to 2010, and in the next decade the EU will see a further substantial increase in its fleet.
As far as goods transport is concerned, growth is due to a large extent to changes in the European economy and its system of production.
In the last 20 years, as internal frontiers have been abolished, the EU has moved from a 'stock' economy to a 'flow' economy.

This phenomenon has been emphasised by the relocation of some industries, particularly those which are labour intensive, to reduce production costs, even though the production site is hundreds or even thousands of kilometres away from the final assembly plant or away from users.
items.explain:
Q15: Paragraph B explains that industries have moved far away from users to cut costs, with production sites *'hundreds or even thousands of kilometres away from the final assembly plant or away from users'*. This directly describes **'changes affecting the distances goods may be transported'**. So the answer is **iii**.

Q23: The passage says industries moved to reduce costs, but the production site is *'hundreds or even thousands of kilometres away from... users'*. This means they moved **farther away** from consumers, not closer. The question says the opposite, so the answer is **FALSE**.

items.sentence_raw: The strong economic growth expected in countries which are candidates for entry to the EU will also increase transport flows, in particular road haulage traffic.
items.explain: Q16: Paragraph C focuses on *'countries which are candidates for entry to the EU'* and how their economic growth will increase transport. This perfectly matches the heading **'transport trends in countries awaiting EU admission'**. So the answer is **xi**.

items.sentence_raw: In 1998, some of these countries already exported more than twice their 1990 volumes and imported more than five times their 1990 volumes.
And although many candidate countries inherited a transport system which encourages rail, the distribution between modes has tipped sharply in favour of road transport since the 1990s.

Between 1990 and 1998, road haulage increased by 19.4%, while during the same period rail haulage decreased by 43.5%, although - and this could benefit the enlarged EU - it is still on average at a much higher level than in existing member states.
However, a new imperative - sustainable development - offers an opportunity for adapting the EU's common transport policy.
items.explain: Q17: Paragraph D introduces *'a new imperative - sustainable development'* as a goal for the EU's transport policy. **'New imperative'** means a fresh and important goal, which matches the heading **'a fresh and important long-term goal'**. So the answer is **i**.

items.sentence_raw: This objective, agreed by the Gothenburg European Council, has to be achieved by integrating environmental considerations into Community policies, and shifting the balance between modes of transport lies at the heart of its strategy.

The ambitious objective can only be fully achieved by 2020, but proposed measures are nonetheless a first essential step towards a sustainable transport system which will ideally be in place in 30 years' time, that is by 2040.
In 1998, energy consumption in the transport sector was to blame for 28% of emissions of CO₂, the leading greenhouse gas.
items.explain: Q18: Paragraph E states that transport was *'to blame for 28% of emissions of CO₂'* and that road transport is the *'main culprit'*. This is all about **'the environmental costs of road transport'**. So the answer is **v**.

items.sentence_raw: According to the latest estimates, if nothing is done to reverse the traffic growth trend, CO₂ emissions from transport can be expected to increase by around 50% to 1,113 billion tonnes by 2020, compared with the 739 billion tonnes recorded in 1990.
items.explain: Q26: The passage predicts CO₂ emissions will increase to *'1,113 billion tonnes by 2020'*, and that the *'739 billion tonnes'* was the level in 1990. The question says emissions will reach 739 billion tonnes by the end of this decade, which is the old number, not the predicted increase. So the answer is **FALSE**.

items.sentence_raw: Once again, road transport is the main culprit since it alone accounts for 84% of the CO₂ emissions attributable to transport.
Using alternative fuels and improving energy efficiency is thus both an ecological necessity and a technological challenge.
At the same time greater efforts must be made to achieve a modal shift.
Such a change cannot be achieved overnight, all the less so after over half a century of constant deterioration in favour of road.

This has reached such a pitch that today rail freight services are facing marginalisation, with just 8% of market share, and with international goods trains struggling along at an average speed of 18km/h.
Three possible options have emerged.
The first approach would consist of focusing on road transport solely through pricing.
items.explain: Q19: Paragraph G describes the first approach which would *'focus on road transport solely through pricing'*. **'Solely'** means only, so this is about **'restricting road use through charging policies alone'**. So the answer is **x**.

items.sentence_raw: This option would not be accompanied by complementary measures in the other modes of transport.

In the short term it might curb the growth in road transport through the better loading ratio of goods vehicles and occupancy rates of passenger vehicles expected as a result of the increase in the price of transport.
However, the lack of measures available to revitalise other modes of transport would make it impossible for more sustainable modes of transport to take up the baton.
The second approach also concentrates on road transport pricing but is accompanied by measures to increase the efficiency of the other modes
items.explain: Q20: Paragraph H says the second approach *'concentrates on road transport pricing but is accompanied by measures to increase the efficiency of the other modes'*. This means **'charging for roads and improving other transport methods'**. So the answer is **ii**.

items.sentence_raw: [better quality of services, logistics, technology].
However, this approach does not include investment in new infrastructure, nor does it guarantee better regional cohesion.

It could help to achieve greater uncoupling than the first approach, but road transport would keep the lion's share of the market and continue to concentrate on saturated arteries, despite being the most polluting of the modes.
It is therefore not enough to guarantee the necessary shift of the balance.
The third approach, which is not new, comprises a series of measures ranging from pricing to revitalising alternative modes of transport and targeting investment in the trans-European network.
items.explain: Q21: Paragraph I describes the third approach which *'comprises a series of measures ranging from pricing to revitalising alternative modes'*. This is a complete plan, matching **'taking all the steps necessary to change transport patterns'**. So the answer is **iv**.

items.sentence_raw: This integrated approach would allow the market shares of the other modes to return to their 1998 levels and thus make a shift of balance.

It is far more ambitious than it looks, bearing in mind the historical imbalance in favour of roads for the last fifty years, but would achieve a marked break in the link between road transport growth and economic growth, without placing restrictions on the mobility of people and goods.

subtitles: What have been the trends and what are the prospects for European transport systems?

orphan_explain_map.24: Q24: The passage discusses transport trends in EU candidate countries but never mentions the **cost of cars** there. ***NOT GIVEN is not the same as FALSE*** — the information about car prices is simply missing. So the answer is **NOT GIVEN**.
orphan_explain_map.25: Q25: The passage mentions the Gothenburg European Council agreed on an objective, but it never says when the council was **set up**. ***Do not confuse the council's creation date with its meeting date***. This information is missing, so the answer is **NOT GIVEN**.
